parts: Do you think that the techniques from the generalized_isothermal_wave_metrics manuscript might be related to a geometric formulation of gravity? One possibility that I've considered is that it could be related to the double copy formulation of general relativity.
I’ll read the manuscript and compare its geometric structure with gravity and the classical double copy, looking for concrete links and where the analogy might break down.

There’s a concrete connection: the manuscript’s metrics already have the Kerr–Schild form used in the classical double copy. The descended connection differs from the usual Kerr–Schild single copy by a transverse derivative. I’m also checking a second link: the bundle transition is the derivative of the gravitational twistor gluing.

Yes. After reading the manuscript, I think there is a **concrete connection to the classical double copy**, and the twistor construction suggests a potentially deeper geometric explanation. The present result already encodes a special sector of vacuum gravity in flat-space gauge data; extending that into a general formulation of gravity remains a substantial further step.

The most immediate connection comes directly from your metric:
\[
g_H=\eta_0+H(u,z)\,k\otimes k,
\qquad
\eta_0=2\,du\,dv+2\,dz\,dw,
\qquad k=du.
\]
This is exactly Kerr–Schild form, with a parallel null covector. The usual classical single-copy prescription associates
\[
\mathcal A_{\mathrm{KS}}=H(u,z)\,du\,\mathsf N
\]
to this metric, choosing your fixed nilpotent matrix as the color generator and suppressing coupling constants. Here it is straightforward to verify the gauge equations: the commutator terms vanish, and
\[
\Box_{\eta_0}H
=2(\partial_u\partial_v+\partial_z\partial_w)H=0.
\]
This is the holomorphic chiral specialization of the pp-wave double copy discussed by [Monteiro, O’Connell and White, §5.1](https://arxiv.org/html/1410.0239v2#S5.SS1).

Comparing this with your descended connection gives a particularly useful identity. Relabel the auxiliary flat coordinates by
\[
(U,V,Z,W)=(-b,c,a,d).
\]
Then your result becomes
\[
A_H=\frac12 H_Z(U,Z)\,dU\,\mathsf N,
\]
so, in these coordinates and the fixed bundle frame,
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
A_H=\frac12\,\partial_Z\mathcal A_{\mathrm{KS}}.}
\]

Thus **your descended spin connection is a transverse derivative of the conventional Kerr–Schild single copy**. This also explains the derivative orders:
\[
F_{\mathrm{KS}}\sim H_Z,\qquad
F_{A_H}\sim H_{ZZ},\qquad
R[g_H]\sim H_{ZZ}.
\]
Your construction preserves the gravitational connection and curvature information, which naturally introduces that extra derivative. This identity is a consequence of your formulas, rather than a claim already established by the cited double-copy paper.

I find the **twistor-level relationship even more interesting**. Your gravitational transition is
\[
(P,Q)=\left(\frac p\zeta,\frac q\zeta+\mathcal T(p,\zeta)\right),
\]
and the gauge-bundle transition is precisely its normalized vertical derivative:
\[
G
=\zeta\,\frac{\partial(P,Q)}{\partial(p,q)}
=I+\zeta\mathcal T_p\,\mathsf N.
\]
This is explicit in [the manuscript’s derivative-bundle construction](</Users/ebbaker/Documents/ChatGPT/Generalized Isothermal Coordinates/manuscript/generalized_isothermal_wave_metrics.tex:368>).

After removing the standard \(\zeta^{-1}\) scaling, the gravitational gluing is the shear
\[
S_\zeta(p,q)=(p,q+\zeta\mathcal T(p,\zeta)).
\]
It preserves \(dp\wedge dq\). Locally, it is a Hamiltonian transformation: with
\[
\{f,g\}=f_p g_q-f_q g_p,
\qquad K_p=\zeta\mathcal T,
\]
the shear is the time-one flow of \(X_K=K_p\partial_q\), and \(G=DS_\zeta\).

That gives a precise geometric sequence:
\[
\text{Hamiltonian twistor gluing}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\text{its action on vertical tangent vectors}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\text{flat-side Ward bundle}
\;\longrightarrow\;
A_H.
\]

This is closely aligned with the Hamiltonian and Poisson structures underlying the self-dual double copy, where gauge-theory color algebra is replaced by a kinematic algebra. That relationship appears in [Monteiro–O’Connell’s kinematic-algebra construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.2565), and actual double-copy constructions on twistor space are developed by [Borsten and collaborators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.10383).

My interpretation is that your method could provide a geometric explanation of how gravitational twistor data generate gauge data. The transfer through the common surface \(B\), together with splitting over complete projective fibers, is what makes this more substantial than simply observing that a spin connection is a gauge connection.

There is also a **Weyl-double-copy interpretation available in this family**. In aligned spin frames, the nonzero Weyl spinor and the color-stripped curvature of \(A_H\) have the forms
\[
\Psi_{ABCD}\propto H_{ZZ}\,o_Ao_Bo_Co_D,
\qquad
f_{AB}\propto H_{ZZ}\,o_Ao_B.
\]
Taking a second, constant aligned Maxwell spinor
\[
\widetilde f_{AB}=o_Ao_B
\]
gives, after fixing constant normalizations,
\[
\Psi_{ABCD}
=\frac{f_{(AB}\widetilde f_{CD)}}{S},
\]
with constant \(S\). Both Maxwell fields satisfy their flat-space equations here. This realizes the *mixed* Weyl-double-copy form described by [Chacón, Nagy and White](https://arxiv.org/html/2103.16441v1#S2.SS1). It depends on the adapted identification of spin frames, so it does not resolve your manuscript’s question about an intrinsic tangent-spinor identification.

The main limitation is that this family makes the relevant algebra unusually simple. Every gauge coefficient lies in \(\mathbb C\mathsf N\), while every overlap Hamiltonian \(K(p,\zeta)\) is independent of \(q\). Consequently,
\[
[A_\mu,A_\nu]=0,
\qquad
\{K_1,K_2\}=0.
\]
The construction therefore supplies an exact classical example, but it does not yet test the nontrivial interaction algebra behind the broader double copy. Likewise, the type-N Weyl factorization is easy enough that its existence alone gives limited evidence for a canonical correspondence.

For a geometric formulation of gravity, I would treat your basic object as **the descended connection together with the incidence and frame data needed to recover spacetime geometry**. Your manuscript already recognizes why this matters: reconstruction from \(A_H\) fixes coordinates and a bundle frame, whereas the twistor-line incidence reconstructs the conformal metric. An arbitrary gauge-equivalence class of ASD connections has not yet been shown to retain all that information.

The next investigation I would prioritize is extending the derivative-of-gluing construction to Hamiltonian transitions depending on **both** fiber coordinates. That would introduce noncommuting Hamiltonian transformations and test whether your transfer mechanism respects the known self-dual double-copy structure. Eguchi–Hanson is a particularly useful comparison because it is already studied, alongside self-dual waves, in [Brown, Gowdy and Spence’s paper cited in your manuscript](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.11063). The key question would be whether the gravitational gluing still produces suitable flat-side bundle data once the common-surface simplification disappears.

I reorganized the folder, and made a subfolder called double copy for this project. Please place any notes within the notes sub-folder there. I want to understand the limitation better. Can you explain in more detail which algebra is simple, the restriction on the overlap Hamiltonian, etc? Please define all of the notation when writing down the restrictions. Does this make the idea kind of bespoke? Is there a way to generalize?

I’ll check the reorganized folder, then unpack the two algebras and where the restriction enters the construction. I’ll put any saved notes in `double copy/notes` and distinguish what can be generalized from what still needs a new argument.

The restriction does two jobs: it makes the relevant brackets vanish, and it supplies the shared coordinates used to transfer the bundle to flat twistor space. That makes the construction special, but not isolated. The wave family sits inside the general heavenly equation, where we can see explicitly which terms return when we perturb beyond it.

There’s a stronger qualification to my earlier Eguchi–Hanson suggestion. If we require the entire pulled-back spin connection to descend to flat spacetime, mixed curvature components give a local obstruction. Eguchi–Hanson cannot satisfy that exact requirement. It remains useful for testing a broader bundle transfer or a double-copy relation, so I’m making that distinction explicit in the notes.

**It is a natural special sector, but the mechanism that transfers the entire connection is more restrictive than my previous answer suggested.** There are two different abelian algebras involved. Their simplification makes the construction explicit; it also hides the interactions one would want to test in a broader double-copy correspondence.

I saved the detailed calculations, including a new obstruction to the strongest generalization, in [double-copy/notes/algebraic_restrictions_and_generalizations.md](</Users/ebbaker/Documents/ChatGPT/Generalized Isothermal Coordinates/double-copy/notes/algebraic_restrictions_and_generalizations.md>).

**On the gauge side, “simple” meant abelian—not “simple Lie algebra.”** Your connection has the form
\[
A=\alpha N,
\qquad
N=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(A\) is a matrix-valued connection one-form and \(\alpha\) is an ordinary scalar one-form.

The ambient algebra is \(\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb C)\): the traceless complex \(2\times2\) matrices, with bracket
\[
[X,Y]=XY-YX.
\]
But the connection uses only
\[
\mathfrak n=\{sN:s\in\mathbb C\},
\qquad
[sN,tN]=0
\]
for any complex numbers \(s,t\). Thus its color algebra is one-dimensional and abelian.

This does **not** mean its curvature vanishes. If \(d\) denotes exterior differentiation, its curvature is
\[
F_A=dA+A\wedge A=d\alpha\,N,
\]
which can be nonzero. What disappears is the matrix-commutator contribution.

The additional identity \(N^2=0\) is a separate simplification: it makes matrix exponentials and inverses terminate after their linear term. Abelianity and nilpotency play different roles.

**On the twistor side, the commuting algebra is infinite-dimensional.** To define the notation:

- \(\zeta\) is a coordinate on one patch of the projective direction sphere \(\mathbb{CP}^1\); the other patch uses \(\mu=1/\zeta\).
- \(p,q\) are the two twistor fiber coordinates over the first direction patch.
- \(P,Q\) are the corresponding coordinates over the second patch.
- \(\mathcal T\) is the scalar function describing the deformation of the gluing.

Your transition is
\[
P=\frac p\zeta,
\qquad
Q=\frac q\zeta+\mathcal T(p,\zeta).
\]
Its key restriction is
\[
\boxed{\partial_q\mathcal T=0.}
\]

Remove the standard \(1/\zeta\) scaling and write
\[
S_\zeta(p,q)=(p,q+s(p,\zeta)),
\qquad
s=\zeta\mathcal T.
\]
This map fixes \(p\) and shifts \(q\). The shift can depend nonlinearly on \(p\).

At **fixed \(\zeta\)**, define the Poisson bracket of two scalar functions \(f,g\) by
\[
\{f,g\}_{\mathrm{vert}}
=
\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\frac{\partial g}{\partial q}
-
\frac{\partial f}{\partial q}\frac{\partial g}{\partial p}.
\]
The subscript “vert” emphasizes that we differentiate only the fiber coordinates \(p,q\). We do not differentiate \(\zeta\), and this is not a bracket on spacetime coordinates.

A Hamiltonian \(K\) is a scalar function generating the vector field
\[
X_K=\{K,\cdot\}_{\mathrm{vert}}
=-K_q\,\partial_p+K_p\,\partial_q,
\]
where subscripts mean partial derivatives.

For your shear, choose a local primitive satisfying
\[
\boxed{K_q=0,\qquad K_p=s=\zeta\mathcal T.}
\]
Then
\[
X_K=s(p,\zeta)\,\partial_q.
\]
Its time-one flow is exactly \(S_\zeta\). “Overlap Hamiltonian” means this generator is defined where the two twistor patches overlap; it need not be a global scalar function on the whole twistor space.

Now take **any two** allowed Hamiltonians \(K_1(p,\zeta)\) and \(K_2(p,\zeta)\). Since neither depends on \(q\),
\[
\{K_1,K_2\}_{\mathrm{vert}}=0.
\]
Their flows commute: each shifts \(q\) by a function of the unchanged coordinate \(p\), so the order of the shifts does not matter.

That is the second abelian algebra. It contains arbitrary holomorphic functions of \(p,\zeta\), so it is infinite-dimensional despite being commuting. Nonlinear coordinate transformations, commuting transformations, and nonzero gravitational curvature are entirely compatible.

**Differentiation connects the two simplifications.** Let \(D\) denote the Jacobian with respect to \(p,q\), holding \(\zeta\) fixed. Your bundle transition matrix is
\[
G=DS_\zeta
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0\\
s_p&1
\end{pmatrix}
=I+\beta N,
\qquad
\beta=s_p=K_{pp},
\]
where \(I\) is the identity matrix.

Thus the commuting Hamiltonian shears produce matrices in the same one-generator subgroup used by the connection. Factoring these matrices becomes an additive splitting problem for the scalar function \(\beta\). This is why the explicit bundle reconstruction is unusually manageable.

There is a further geometric benefit: both the curved and flat twistor spaces can forget \(q\) and project to the same surface \(B\), whose coordinates are \((p,\zeta)\). Since \(G\) depends only on those coordinates, it defines a bundle on \(B\) that can be pulled back to either twistor space.

This restriction is built into that particular bridge. If we insist on keeping \(P=p/\zeta\) and preserving the fiber symplectic structure with its required scaling,
\[
d_{\mathrm{vert}}P\wedge d_{\mathrm{vert}}Q
=\zeta^{-2}dp\wedge dq,
\]
where \(d_{\mathrm{vert}}\) differentiates only fiber coordinates, then necessarily
\[
Q_q=\frac1\zeta,
\]
and therefore
\[
Q=\frac q\zeta+\mathcal T(p,\zeta).
\]
So **retaining this exact common projection forces the shear form**. Adding general \(q\)-dependence requires changing the transfer mechanism.

Does that make the idea bespoke? I would call it **a natural but strongly reduced model**. It covers arbitrary profiles \(H(u,z)\), and its defining geometric condition—two parallel vector fields spanning a totally null plane—is intrinsic. However, its explicit connection transfer depends materially on that special geometry.

Also, abelianity does not disqualify a classical double copy. Familiar Kerr–Schild double copies already involve fixed-color Maxwell fields. The limitation is that your family cannot test the replacement of **nonzero** color brackets by **nonzero** kinematic brackets. [Monteiro, O’Connell and White discuss this explicitly for pp-waves.](https://arxiv.org/html/1410.0239v2#S5.SS1)

**There are concrete ways to move beyond the commuting sector.** Allow Hamiltonians to depend on both fiber coordinates. For example,
\[
K_1=\frac{p^3}{3},
\qquad
K_2=\frac{q^3}{3}
\]
give
\[
\{K_1,K_2\}_{\mathrm{vert}}=p^2q^2\ne0.
\]
Their flows move different coordinates and generally do not commute. These are local algebra examples; a complete twistor construction must also satisfy the appropriate patching and twistor-line conditions.

General Hamiltonian gluing belongs naturally to the broader twistor description of self-dual gravity. But one must retain the movement of the evaluation point when differentiating it. For fiber maps \(\Phi,\Psi\) and a fiber point \(\xi=(p,q)\),
\[
D(\Phi\circ\Psi)(\xi)
=
D\Phi(\Psi(\xi))\,D\Psi(\xi).
\]
The derivative construction therefore involves more than multiplying matrix-valued functions at the same point. Your shear family suppresses this complication because the coordinate on which its Jacobians depend is unchanged. Broader twistor double-copy constructions explicitly incorporate richer algebraic structures. [Borsten and collaborators provide one such construction.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.10383)

A particularly concrete extension is available through the **heavenly equation**. Let \(u,v,z,w\) be spacetime coordinates and \(\Theta(u,v,z,w)\) a scalar potential. Define
\[
\Box_0=2(\partial_u\partial_v+\partial_z\partial_w).
\]
In an appropriate gravitational potential gauge, the equation is
\[
\mathcal E(\Theta)
:=
\Box_0\Theta-\Theta_{zz}\Theta_{vv}+(\Theta_{vz})^2=0.
\]
Here \(\mathcal E\) names the expression on the right, and subscripts again denote partial derivatives. These conventions are obtained from [Brown, Gowdy and Spence](https://arxiv.org/html/2307.11063v2#S2.SS2) by a coordinate relabeling.

Your metric
\[
g_H=2du\,dv+2dz\,dw+H(u,z)du^2
\]
corresponds to a potential \(\Theta_0(u,z)\) satisfying
\[
\Theta_{0,zz}=H.
\]
Because \(\Theta_0\) depends only on \(u,z\), both the linear and quadratic heavenly terms vanish separately.

Now introduce a general perturbation \(\chi(u,v,z,w)\) and a formal small parameter \(\epsilon\). Direct substitution gives
\[
\mathcal E(\Theta_0+\epsilon\chi)
=
\epsilon\bigl(\Box_0\chi-H\chi_{vv}\bigr)
+
\epsilon^2\bigl((\chi_{vz})^2-\chi_{zz}\chi_{vv}\bigr).
\]
This displays precisely what the wave restriction hides. Perturbations outside the family can activate the quadratic term while remaining within self-dual gravity. They must, of course, satisfy the resulting equations; arbitrary perturbations are not automatically solutions.

**There is also a stronger obstruction to preserving the full transport prescription unchanged.** This is a deduction from the curvature, and it sharpens my earlier suggestion about Eguchi–Hanson.

Write \(x(y,\zeta)\) for the source spacetime point selected by an inverse generalized chart, where \(y\) collectively denotes the four flat spacetime coordinates. Let \(R^S\) be the curvature of the source chiral spin connection, and define
\[
x_\zeta=\frac{\partial x}{\partial\zeta}\Big|_y.
\]
If the **entire pulled-back connection** is to be gauge-equivalent to a connection depending only on \(y\), its curvature must satisfy
\[
\boxed{
R^S(x_\zeta,\xi)=0
\quad\text{for every source tangent vector }\xi.
}
\]
A change of bundle frame cannot remove a violation of this condition, because it only conjugates the curvature.

Your wave construction satisfies it: changing \(\zeta\) moves the source point only in the \(v,w\) directions, whereas
\[
R^S=\frac12H_{zz}\,dz\wedge du\,N
\]
annihilates those directions.

For curvature with no such annihilating direction, the condition forces \(x_\zeta=0\). Combined with preservation of the chiral null two-planes, that would make the chart an ordinary conformal map to flat spacetime, contradicting nonzero Weyl curvature.

In Ricci-flat ASD geometry, the argument sharpens to a necessary condition of **Petrov type N or O**: respectively, four coincident principal spinors, or zero Weyl curvature. The derivation is in the saved notes. Eguchi–Hanson is type D, with two distinct double principal spinors, so it cannot satisfy this unchanged full-pullback requirement. Its established double copies are unaffected because they make a different claim. [Luna and collaborators describe those copies.](https://arxiv.org/html/1810.08183v3#S5)

I would therefore pursue a generalization that transfers the **twistor bundle or transport along the chiral null planes**, retaining the incidence data needed to reconstruct the metric. Requiring equality with the whole pulled-back Levi–Civita connection is substantially stronger and encounters the obstruction above. The most informative first calculation would be a heavenly perturbation through second order, where nonzero interactions appear, followed by checking exactly which notion of geometric transport survives.
Is R^S the Ricci curvature? So the generalization works for Ricci flat manifolds?

No—**\(R^S\) is the curvature of the spin connection, not the Ricci curvature.** I should have made that distinction clearer.

Here \(S\) denotes the rank-two spinor bundle, and \(\gamma\) is its connection. Its curvature is the matrix-valued two-form
\[
R^S=d\gamma+\gamma\wedge\gamma.
\]
The superscript \(S\) labels the bundle on which the curvature acts.

The **Ricci tensor** is a contraction of the full Riemann curvature tensor. Setting it to zero leaves the Weyl curvature—the part describing vacuum gravitational curvature—potentially nonzero. In the manuscript’s Ricci-flat, anti-self-dual setting, \(R^S\) encodes that remaining Weyl curvature. Thus
\[
\operatorname{Ric}(g)=0
\quad\text{does not imply}\quad
R^S=0.
\]

For example, your profile \(H=z^2\) gives a Ricci-flat metric, but its Riemann curvature has
\[
R_{uzuz}=-1.
\]
Its spin curvature is nonzero too.

**Consequently, Ricci-flatness alone does not make the proposed generalization work.** There are three different statements:

- Your manuscript establishes the construction for the special wave class with two parallel null vector fields.
- The broader gravitational twistor framework accommodates general holomorphic Ricci-flat, anti-self-dual metrics.
- Transferring their connections to flat spacetime with the manuscript’s precise compatibility properties requires further work. The obstruction we discussed applies even within that Ricci-flat class.

The crucial condition is that \(R^S\) **annihilate the directions in which the generalized chart moves the source point**. Your wave metrics have those directions. Ricci-flat metrics in general do not.
When you write the curvature of the spin connection, are you still in the Twistor picture? Can you translate that back to the usual picture?

**\(R^S\) is already a curvature on spacetime.** It is written in spinor notation; twistor space is not needed to define it. Twistor theory enters when we construct the direction-dependent maps and transfer the connection.

In the usual tensor picture, start with the Levi–Civita covariant derivative \(\nabla\). Its curvature measures the failure of covariant derivatives to commute:
\[
R(X,Y)V
=
\nabla_X\nabla_YV-\nabla_Y\nabla_XV-\nabla_{[X,Y]}V,
\]
where \(X,Y,V\) are vector fields and \([X,Y]\) is their Lie bracket.

In coordinates \(x^\mu\), this becomes
\[
[\nabla_\mu,\nabla_\nu]V^\rho
=
R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}V^\sigma.
\]
Here Greek indices label the four spacetime coordinates, repeated indices are summed, and \(R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}\) is the ordinary **Riemann curvature tensor**.

The Ricci tensor is its contraction:
\[
\operatorname{Ric}_{\sigma\nu}
=
R^\rho{}_{\sigma\rho\nu}.
\]
Thus Ricci-flatness sets a contraction to zero, while the full curvature can remain nonzero.

**The spin connection describes this same geometry using spinors instead of tangent vectors.** One can express the Levi–Civita connection in coordinate frames, in tetrad frames—a tetrad is a local basis of tangent vectors—or in spinor frames.

In four complex dimensions, tangent vectors have two spinor factors:
\[
TM\simeq S\otimes S'.
\]
Here \(TM\) is the tangent bundle, and \(S,S'\) are the two rank-two spinor bundles. The Levi–Civita connection induces connections on both factors. Their curvatures are called \(R^S\) and \(R^{S'}\).

For your manuscript’s metrics, the connection on \(S'\) is flat. Consequently, **\(R^S\) contains all the nonzero Riemann curvature information**. In this particular class, we can translate the condition involving \(R^S\) directly into an ordinary Riemann-tensor condition.

To do that, write
\[
x^\mu=x^\mu(y,\zeta)
\]
for the source spacetime point selected by an inverse generalized chart. Here \(y\) denotes the four auxiliary flat-spacetime coordinates, and \(\zeta\) labels the additional direction. Holding \(y\) fixed and varying \(\zeta\) traces a curve in the source spacetime, with tangent
\[
v^\mu=\frac{\partial x^\mu}{\partial\zeta}\Big|_y.
\]

The necessary condition for the **entire transported connection** to descend to flat spacetime is, in ordinary tensor notation,
\[
\boxed{
v^\mu R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}=0
\quad\text{for every }\rho,\sigma,\nu.
}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
R(v,X)V=0
\]
for every pair of tangent vectors \(X,V\).

This says that the direction-dependent chart may move the source point only along directions annihilated by the full curvature tensor. It is a much stronger and different condition than vanishing Ricci curvature.

Your wave metric makes this concrete:
\[
g_H=2\,du\,dv+2\,dz\,dw+H(u,z)\,du^2,
\]
where \(u,v,z,w\) are spacetime coordinates and \(H\) is the profile. Its curvature is generated by
\[
R_{uzuz}=-\frac12H_{zz},
\qquad
H_{zz}=\frac{\partial^2H}{\partial z^2}.
\]
Nevertheless,
\[
R(\partial_v,X)=0,
\qquad
R(\partial_w,X)=0
\]
for every tangent vector \(X\).

Your generalized chart changes the source point only in those \(v,w\) directions when the auxiliary direction varies. That is why it can retain nonzero gravitational curvature while satisfying the descent condition.

So the restriction has an ordinary spacetime interpretation: **the chart’s direction-dependent motion must lie in the common kernel of the Riemann curvature.** Twistor methods construct the chart, but this necessary condition can be stated entirely in conventional differential geometry.
Wait, if the Ricci curvature vanishes, wouldn't that condition be satifsied? How is it stronger?
I’ll make the difference explicit with a Ricci-flat example where the required curvature contraction is nonzero.

**No: Ricci-flatness says a trace of the curvature vanishes. The condition we need says that the curvature annihilates a particular vector.** Taking a trace loses information.

A matrix analogy is
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its trace is zero, but \(M V\neq0\) for every nonzero vector \(V\). “Trace-free” does not mean “has a kernel.”

For curvature, the two operations are:

\[
\underbrace{\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}
=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd}=0}_{\text{Ricci-flatness}},
\qquad
\underbrace{\sum_c V^cR_{abcd}=0
\ \text{for every }a,b,d}_{\text{required curvature-kernel condition}}.
\]

Here \(R_{abcd}\) is the Riemann tensor with all indices lowered, \(g^{ac}\) is the inverse metric, and \(V\) is the direction in which the generalized chart moves the source point. Each index ranges over the four spacetime coordinates.

The first expression sums over **two curvature indices using the inverse metric**. The second inserts **a vector into one curvature slot**, leaving every other component required to vanish. These are different contractions.

Your own example makes the distinction explicit. Take
\[
g=2\,du\,dv+2\,dz\,dw+z^2du^2.
\]
This metric satisfies
\[
\operatorname{Ric}=0,
\qquad
R_{uzuz}=-1.
\]
If \(V=\partial_u\), meaning its \(u\)-component is one and its other components vanish, then
\[
\sum_c V^cR_{uzcz}=R_{uzuz}=-1\neq0.
\]
So the required condition fails for that direction, despite Ricci-flatness.

There is no contradiction with the Ricci contraction. For instance,
\[
\operatorname{Ric}_{zz}=g^{uu}R_{uzuz}=0,
\]
because this metric has \(g^{uu}=0\). The trace does not detect that nonzero component.

**My word “stronger” was imprecise.** More accurately, curvature nullity is an **additional condition within the already Ricci-flat class**. For one specified vector, it is not a condition that by itself implies the entire Ricci tensor vanishes.

Your construction works because its direction-dependent motion lies along \(\partial_v,\partial_w\), which the curvature does annihilate. It would fail if that motion instead lay along \(\partial_u\). **That special alignment—not Ricci-flatness alone—is the extra ingredient.**

I added this explicit distinction to the [notes](</Users/ebbaker/Documents/ChatGPT/Generalized Isothermal Coordinates/double-copy/notes/algebraic_restrictions_and_generalizations.md>).
Oh sorry is R the full Riemann tensor in your notation?

Yes—**\(R_{abcd}\) is the full Riemann curvature tensor** in my notation.

- \(\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=g^{ac}R_{abcd}\) is the **Ricci tensor**, obtained by contraction.
- \(R^S\) is the curvature of the **spin connection**; for your manuscript’s metrics, it encodes all the nonzero Riemann curvature.
- For a Ricci-flat metric, the full Riemann tensor equals the **Weyl tensor**, which can still be nonzero.

I should have kept those notational distinctions clearer.
Sorry I thought it referred to Ric
No problem—I introduced several closely related curvature symbols too quickly. I’ll use \(\mathrm{Riem}\) for the full Riemann tensor and \(\mathrm{Ric}\) for the Ricci tensor from here on.

The main structure is now clear: a local curvature criterion explains both why the wave construction works and why the same full-connection transfer cannot extend to arbitrary Ricci-flat metrics. The review has clarified an important distinction: the patchwise generalized charts themselves extend to much broader twistor geometries. The obstruction concerns carrying the entire gravitational connection through those charts. I’m making that separation central to the draft so that the limits of one transfer prescription do not appear to rule out the broader geometric idea.

The full draft is written. I’m now checking the proofs, notation, references, and rendered pages. The final section separates three open questions: which type N metrics admit full descent, how to make the broader bundle transfer independent of chart choices, and whether that transfer reproduces nonzero interaction terms.

The draft now develops the curvature obstruction, the wave construction, its double-copy identities, and the routes beyond the wave sector. The proof reviews and PDF checks are complete; I’m saving the final 20-page PDF alongside the editable source in `double-copy`.
